---
title: "Cardiometabolic Complications In Pregnancy And Biological Ageing In The Offspring: A Systematic Review And Meta-Analysis"
description: Maternal cardiometabolic complications during pregnancy, such as higher maternal BMI, are associated with changes in offspring biological aging markers, including shorter telomere length and altered DNA methylation patterns.
author: Gemini
date: 2026-11-02
categories: [Lever, Analytical]
---
New research sheds light on how a mother's health during pregnancy can influence her child's biological aging. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis explored the link between cardiometabolic complications in expectant mothers and markers of biological aging in their offspring. These complications include conditions like gestational diabetes, high blood pressure during pregnancy, and higher maternal body mass index (BMI).

The study investigated two key indicators of biological aging: telomere length and DNA methylation. Telomeres are protective caps at the ends of our chromosomes, and their length is often seen as a marker of cellular aging; shorter telomeres are generally linked to faster aging. DNA methylation refers to chemical tags on our DNA that can switch genes on or off, playing a crucial role in how our bodies function and age.

The findings suggest that while gestational diabetes and high blood pressure during pregnancy didn't show a clear link to offspring telomere length, a higher maternal BMI was associated with slightly shorter telomeres in children. More significantly, exposure to these cardiometabolic complications was connected to abnormal DNA methylation patterns in genes important for heart and metabolic health. Specifically, higher methylation levels were observed in umbilical cord blood and placental tissue after exposure to diabetes and high blood pressure.

This research highlights the profound impact of the intrauterine environment on a child's long-term health trajectory, suggesting that maternal health during pregnancy could influence how quickly a child's body ages at a cellular level. Understanding these connections could pave the way for interventions to promote healthier aging from the very beginning of life.
